newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Kofi Annan of Ghana is next U.N. secretary-general.
newsitem.headline: Kofi Annan of Ghana is next U.N. secretary-general.

text.p: Kofi Annan, a career U.N. diplomat from Ghana, was chosen by the Security Council on Friday to be the next U.N. secretary-general, succeeding Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali whose hopes for a second term were derailed by Washington.

The soft-spoken 58-year-old Annan, undersecretary-general for peace-keeping operations, won the support of all 15 Security Council members after France dropped a veto threat. The choice now goes to the 185-nation General Assembly, which will appoint him on Tuesday.
Annan will become the seventh secretary general in U.N. history and the first from sub-Sahara Africa. He will also be the first secretary general to rise through U.N. ranks.
He takes up the $205,809 a year post January 1, 1997. The perks of one of the world's toughest jobs include a town house overlooking the East River on New York's posh Upper East Side.
He will succeed Boutros-Ghali, the 74-year-old Egyptian former deputy prime minister who wanted a second five-year term but was elbowed out by the United States.
Washington said the United Nations needs new leadership to carry out reforms and since June has spent much diplomatic capital and goodwill to block his re-election.

Boutros-Ghali stepped aside after being vetoed by American U.N. envoy Madeleine Albright in a November 19 Security Council vote in which he was the only candidate. The Ghanaian diplomat then entered the contest, along with three other Africans from French-speaking countries.
In a statement after receiving the council's nod, Annan said: "My highest priority will be to work with all member states to redefine the objectives of the organisation in the post-Cold War world."
Aware of the shortcomings for which the middle-aged United Nations has been blamed, he said it was "time to agree on what the United Nations can and must do, and what it cannot do."

Annan has served for more than 30 years in posts as far afield as Addis Ababa, Geneva, Cairo and New York. After Iraq's invasion of Kuwait he was sent to the region to help extricate more than 900 international staff. He also became engaged in the release of Western hostages and helped resolve the plight of over 500,000 stranded Asians in Kuwait and Iraq.
Annan has headed U.N. peacekeeping since early 1993, during a time when it grew to more than 70,000 troops serving from Somalia and Bosnia to Rwanda and Haiti.
Despite criticism in many quarters, including the United States, over the handling of some operations, most of it was directed at Boutros-Ghali rather than Annan.
With the United Nations sometimes accused of biting off more than it can chew, Annan said charting its future would require consensus and cooperation among all member states.

One of his biggest headaches will be trying to solve the organisation's perpetual bankruptcy, with unpaid dues and peacekeeping costs often well above the $2 billion mark. The United States, assessed 25 percent of the annual $1.3 billion budget and an even bigger percentage for peacekeeping, is also the biggest debtor.

"In January, we must embark upon a time for healing -- to restore confidence between governments and this institution in order to help replenish its financial strength and its political and moral authority," Annan said.
U.S. ambassador Albright, recently nominated to be President Bill Clinton's new Secretary of State, hailed Annan's election, saying: "It has been a good and successful process and I am very pleased."

She also complimented Boutros-Ghali, whose re-election she blocked, praising the "job and the hard work (he) has in fact performed during his term. He is a renowned international statesman and has made his mark in history," she said.
Boutros-Ghali said he was pleased the council's decision was unanimous and gratified that Africa was able to maintain the office of secretary-general for a second five-year term.

According to an unwritten tradition, a U.N. chief is usually given two five-year terms. Since the United States barred Boutros-Ghali from a second term, the council gave priority to other candidates from Africa.

The diplomatic manoeuvring which preceded Annan's selection added to already bruised feelings on a number of issues between the United States and France, which had backed Boutros-Ghali and resented Washington's veto.

When Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy earlier this month, France switched to supporting candidates from French-speaking African countries and was the last to line up behind Annan after casting vetoes in informal ballots.
If it had persisted in opposing Annan, the contest could have been thrown open to other regions, earning the resentment of many Africans.
